title: How do you clean up an oil spill?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how oil spills are cleaned up, prompted by the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill in the Gulf of Mexico. They cover the spill's size and comparisons to the Exxon Valdez and the Persian Gulf War spill, then methods including hair sorbents, booms and skimmers, burning, natural evaporation and photodegradation, microbial bioremediation with nutrients, chemical dispersants and their harms, tar balls, beach cleanup with high-pressure hoses, and wildlife deterrence. The episode closes with listener mail, thanks to sponsors, New York live event announcements, and a donation plug for CoEd in Guatemala.

segments.title: Opening banter and oil spill introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the show and the Gulf oil spill, and Chuck mentions having written an article on oil spill cleanup in 2006 after a San Francisco Bay spill.

segments.title: Deepwater Horizon spill and its size
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Deepwater Horizon explosion during well capping, which killed eleven people and sank the rig, and the uncertain estimates of the leaking oil, which may be far above the official 5,000 barrels a day. They compare the spill to the Exxon Valdez and the Persian Gulf War spill, and give statistics on US oil use and spill rates.

segments.title: Hair sorbents and tanker regulations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea of using donated hair to soak up oil, noting BP judged it not feasible for the large spill though hair is used on smaller spills. They also mention post-Exxon Valdez tanker design rules and a reported drop in spillage.

segments.title: Blowout preventer requirements and energy policy
segments.summary: Chuck relays that other countries use a subsea shut-off process that seals a well automatically, which the US dropped for cost reasons, and they note the MMS relationship with energy companies and the effect of the West Virginia mine explosion on energy policy.

segments.title: Sorbents, booms, and skimmers
segments.summary: The hosts explain sorbents as materials that soak up oil, how oil forms a thin layer on water, and how booms with skirts contain slicks while skimmers, including centripetal and conveyor-belt types, remove oil. They note natural sorbents such as pine bark and banana fibers, and that the oil soaked up can be squeezed out and reused.

segments.title: Burning, evaporation, and natural breakdown
segments.summary: The hosts describe in-situ burning as efficient when a slick is far from shore and coral, but producing noxious fumes. They discuss leaving distant slicks to evaporate and photodegrade, with volatile compounds mostly gone within about 24 to 48 hours, though continuous new leakage complicates this.

segments.title: Bioremediation and chemical dispersants
segments.summary: The hosts explain adding nitrogen and phosphorus to encourage oil-eating microbes, with the risk of algae blooms and dead zones offshore. They then describe chemical dispersants that break oil into droplets and an Israeli study finding dispersant-treated oil more harmful to coral than crude oil.

segments.title: Wildlife impacts, tar balls, beach cleanup, and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how broken-down oil enters the seafood chain, forms tar balls, and harms birds and mammals. They describe high-pressure hose beach cleanup in Prince William Sound that pushed oil into sand, and deterrents like scarecrows used around cleanup boats. The episode then moves to listener mail, New York event announcements, and a CoEd donation plug.
